articles.title: The one line that explains a prompt edit
articles.excerpt: Most prompt edits are reactions. A reply misses in some specific way, and a line goes in to stop it happening again. The edit is small. The reason behind it is the useful part, and it's usually gone w…
articles.body: Most prompt edits are reactions. A reply misses in some specific way, and a line goes in to stop it happening again. The edit is small. The reason behind it is the useful part, and it's usually gone within a week. Edits without reasons pile up A prompt that has been edited a dozen times becomes a list of rules with no explanations. Some still matter. Some were fixes for one odd input. From the outside they look identical, so nobody dares remove any of them, and the prompt only ever grows. One line per edit The fix is cheap: when you change a prompt, write one line saying why. "Return plain text": output was pasted into a CMS that broke on markdown. Removed the word limit: short answers were dropping the caveats. Format: what changed, a colon, what was going wrong.

A cut that lives in the request path survives the whole demo. This build log wires an expiry timestamp into every feature flag, so an unfinished feature stops answering requests on its own — no 1 a.m. redeploy, no verbal promise to remember to disable it. The demo is deliberately small: a text utility with three AI-backed features behind one free server instance. The constraint is the interesting part. articles.body: To see an Amazon product's past prices today, use Keepa or camelcamelcamel: both chart price history on the product page and send price-drop alerts. To own the data instead (any Amazon storefront or other retailer, your own schedule, raw rows in your database), schedule a scraper and append every reading to SQLite. Your own history starts the day you start, so begin before you need it. This guide covers what the two trackers offer, when your own history is the better choice, and a tested Python pipeline: E-commerce Product Scraper Pro runs on Apify, rows go into SQLite, and a report prints the daily minimum and median with a step chart.

articles.title: PostHog Dropped ClickHouse for DuckDB: A Data Engineer's Take
articles.excerpt: I once watched a single analyst's 14-way join freeze a shared warehouse for a whole company on a Monday morning. Dashboards timed out, the CFO's report never showed up, and 3 teams spent the afternoon…
articles.body: I once watched a single analyst's 14-way join freeze a shared warehouse for a whole company on a Monday morning. Dashboards timed out, the CFO's report never showed up, and 3 teams spent the afternoon blaming each other. That's why I read PostHog's June 29, 2026 engineering post closely. They pulled their managed warehouse off a multi-tenant ClickHouse cluster and gave every organization its own DuckDB instance. The instances sleep when idle, the data sits on S3 through DuckLake, and a Postgres wire endpoint lets ordinary tools connect. The headline sounds like "ClickHouse lost," and that's the wrong read. The post publishes zero benchmarks. PostHog's decision comes down to matching the engine to the shape of the workload, and that's the same reasoning a system design interview tests.

articles.title: NASA closes the book on epic OSIRIS-REx asteroid-sampling mission: 'I am immensely proud of what we did'
articles.excerpt: NASA's OSIRIS-REx asteroid-sampling mission formally ended on Sept. 30, 2026, though scientists will continue to study the pieces of space rock it returned for decades.
articles.body: On Sept. 30, NASA formally concluded OSIRIS-REx, the historic first U.S. mission to pluck a pristine piece of an asteroid and deliver it safely back to Earth. The van-sized OSIRIS-REx spacecraft — whose name is short for Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, Security-Regolith Explorer — visited and sampled Bennu , an ancient space rock holding pristine remnants from the dawn of our solar system more than 4.5 billion years ago. Among those cosmic relics are raw organic building blocks , the kind that may have seeded life on Earth. "I have known this day was coming for a long time, but it is still difficult to see it arrive," OSIRIS-REx Principal Investigator Dante Lauretta, who's based at the University of Arizona, said in a post on LinkedIn .
